item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports balancing negative difficulty with reliability. [Hard-BPR (2024 preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19276) argues ordinary BPR is poorly suited to dynamic hard sampling and modifies the objective to mitigate false-negative influence. [EMM (2026)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0893608026004090) combines hard and random negatives with ID exclusion and similarity-window filtering, excluding excessively close and distant candidates; its evidence concerns contrastive recommendation, not directly BERT4Rec masked prediction. A [2024 sequential-recommendation study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) compares random, popularity, in-batch and adaptive sampling, finding dataset-dependent trade-offs and popularity-band imbalances. Harder sampling is therefore a hypothesis to validate, rather than an assured improvement.\n\nFor the constrained BERT4Rec experiment, a plausible adaptation is masked-target multi-negative cross-entropy with a bounded candidate pool scored by the current model, retaining random negatives alongside moderately hard candidates. Exclude padding, mask IDs, the target and known training-history positives; consider downweighting extreme suspected false negatives rather than treating every high-scoring unseen item as certainly negative. These are proposed adaptations, not established results on the four Amazon categories. Distinguish candidate-set cross-entropy from an importance-corrected approximation to full softmax: adaptive top-k selection changes the sampling distribution. [A 2025 loss analysis](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/11228603) shows ranking-surrogate relationships depend on negative sampling; its NDCG/MRR results do not establish HR@10 gains. Preserve bidirectional masked training, appended-mask inference and one checkpoint per category; select using the pinned macro validation HR@10."}
